title: Do Wine Filters Work? An Honest Look at PureWine, Üllo and Drops
excerpt: Do wine filters and drops stop wine headaches? What PureWine, Üllo and sulfite drops actually remove, what the evidence says, and what helps more.
metaDescription: Do wine filters work for headaches? What PureWine, Üllo and sulfite drops remove, why sulfites are rarely the cause, and what helps more.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** wine filters and drops do what they say on the chemistry level. Most of them really do remove sulfites, and some also pull out histamine. What nobody has shown is that this stops wine headaches. For most people, sulfites aren't what causes the headache in the first place, and the filters leave behind the thing most likely to be responsible: the alcohol itself. If you happen to be sensitive to histamine or sulfites, a filter might help a bit. If your headache comes from how much you drank, or from compounds in red grape skins like quercetin, a filter probably won't make much difference.

**The quick version for shoppers:** a sulfite filter or drops are a cheap experiment, not a fix. If you want to try one, test it honestly. Drink the same wine, the same amount, on two different nights, once filtered and once not, and see whether anything changes. Before you spend money, look at the other things in this guide: how much you pour, how fast you drink, whether you eat, how much water you have, and which wines you choose. Those usually matter more.

> **This is not medical advice.** This guide covers general research and product claims. It does not replace a doctor who knows your health history. **See a doctor if** wine (or any food or drink) gives you wheezing, chest tightness, hives, swelling of the lips or throat, or trouble breathing. Those are allergy-type reactions, and a filter is not a safe way to manage them. Also see a doctor if you get headaches after even small amounts of alcohol, if your headaches are getting worse or more frequent, or if you have migraines that alcohol seems to set off. Call 911 for trouble breathing, throat swelling, or a sudden, severe "worst headache of my life."

## What Wine Filters and Drops Actually Do

Wine "purifiers" come in three main forms. They all target the same two compounds, sulfites and histamines, but they work in different ways.

### 1. Stir-in wands (PureWine The Wand)

PureWine's Wand is a single-use stick that you stir into a glass of wine. The company says the wand contains a food-safe resin that grabs histamines and sulfites as the wine moves past it. The idea is that you leave it in the glass for a few minutes and then drink. Because each wand handles one glass, the cost adds up over time if you drink regularly.

### 2. Pour-through filters (PureWine The Wave, Üllo)

These sit on or in the bottle, or over the glass, and filter the wine as you pour.

- **PureWine The Wave** is a single-use pourer that fits a bottle and filters as you pour. It uses the same idea as the Wand, aimed at histamines and sulfites.
- **Üllo** is a reusable device that you hold over a glass or decanter. You pour the wine through a replaceable filter cartridge. Üllo's main claim is sulfite removal. The company says its filter uses a polymer that selectively captures sulfites, and you can adjust the flow to also aerate the wine. Üllo is mostly marketed as a sulfite remover rather than a histamine remover.

### 3. Drops (SO2GO and similar)

Wine drops are a small bottle of liquid you add to the glass or bottle. Most sulfite drops are based on a food-grade, very dilute **hydrogen peroxide** solution. The chemistry here is simple and well understood: hydrogen peroxide reacts with sulfite and turns it into sulfate, a related compound that doesn't act as a preservative and isn't associated with sulfite reactions. A few drops are enough because there's very little sulfite in a glass of wine to begin with.

Drops do not remove histamine. They only target sulfites.

## Do Wine Filters Work? It Depends What "Work" Means

There are two different questions here, and they get blurred in the marketing.

**Question 1: Do they remove sulfites and histamines?** Mostly yes. Hydrogen peroxide drops chemically convert sulfites, and resin or polymer filters can bind them. Manufacturers publish their own test figures showing large reductions. Those numbers come from the companies themselves, not independent labs, so treat the exact percentages with some caution. The basic principle is sound, though.

**Question 2: Do they stop wine headaches?** This is the one you actually care about, and the answer is that there's no good evidence either way. We couldn't find any published, independent clinical trial that tested whether people who drink filtered wine get fewer headaches than people who drink the same wine unfiltered. The customer reviews you'll see are real experiences, but they can't separate the filter's effect from the placebo effect, a lighter pour that night, more water, or a different wine.

The second question depends on something more basic: what actually causes wine headaches. If sulfites and histamine aren't the main cause for you, removing them won't help much.

## Are Sulfites the Real Cause of Wine Headaches?

For most people, probably not. This is the big weakness in the whole product category.

Here's what's well established about sulfites:

- **Sulfite sensitivity is real but uncommon.** The US Food and Drug Administration has estimated that roughly 1% of people are sensitive to sulfites, with a higher rate among people who have asthma. That's why US wines with more than 10 parts per million of sulfites must say "Contains Sulfites" on the label.
- **The usual reaction is breathing trouble, not a headache.** Sulfite reactions most often look like wheezing, chest tightness, or asthma flare-ups, sometimes with hives or flushing. Headache has never been shown to be a typical sulfite reaction.
- **White wine usually has more sulfites than red.** Red wine contains tannins and other compounds that help protect it, so winemakers generally add less. Yet red wine is the one most people blame for headaches. If sulfites were the main cause, white wine should be the bigger problem.
- **Many common foods have much more sulfite than wine.** Dried fruit like apricots, some packaged potato products, and some shrimp can carry far more sulfite per serving than a glass of wine. People rarely report headaches from dried apricots.

None of this means sulfites never matter. If you have asthma and react to dried fruit, sulfites in wine could also affect you, and you should talk to your doctor rather than rely on a filter. But for the typical "red wine gives me a headache" complaint, sulfites are a weak suspect. Our full breakdown is in [sulfites in wine and headaches](/never-hungover/sulfites-in-wine-headaches).

## What About Histamine?

Histamine is a more plausible suspect than sulfites, and it's the reason PureWine targets both.

Histamine forms during fermentation, and red wines generally have more of it than whites, though levels vary a lot from bottle to bottle. Your gut breaks down histamine from food and drink with an enzyme called **diamine oxidase (DAO)**. Some people have low DAO activity, and for them, histamine from food and drink can build up and cause flushing, a stuffy nose, headaches, or hives. Alcohol may also interfere with how well DAO works, so wine is a double hit: it brings histamine in and may slow down how fast you clear it.

The research on wine histamine and headaches is mixed. Some small studies have found that people who report wine intolerance react more to high-histamine wine, while others haven't found a clear link between a wine's histamine content and symptoms. So histamine may matter for some people, especially those who also react to aged cheese, cured meats, or fermented foods, but it doesn't explain every wine headache.

If histamine is your issue, a filter that removes it might genuinely help. You'd still want to confirm it with a real side-by-side test. Our guide to [histamine intolerance and alcohol](/never-hungover/histamine-intolerance-and-alcohol) explains the signs and what else can help.

## The Suspects Filters Don't Touch

These are the likelier causes of most wine headaches, and none of them are removed by sulfite or histamine filters.

### The alcohol itself

Alcohol is the main ingredient in a wine headache. It widens blood vessels, it makes you pee more and can leave you dehydrated, it disrupts your sleep, and your body breaks it down into **acetaldehyde**, a toxic compound linked to headaches, nausea, and flushing. A standard glass of wine is about 5 ounces, and many home pours and restaurant glasses are bigger than that. Higher-alcohol wines (some Zinfandels, Shirazes, and big Californian reds can reach 15% or more) deliver more alcohol per glass than a 12% wine.

Filters and drops do not remove alcohol. A filtered bottle of 15% wine is still a bottle of 15% wine.

### Quercetin in red grape skins

A 2023 study from researchers at the University of California, Davis, published in *Scientific Reports*, proposed a new explanation for red wine headaches. Red grapes, especially those grown in strong sunlight, contain a flavonoid called **quercetin**. When you drink it, your body converts it into a form (quercetin glucuronide) that, in lab tests, blocked the enzyme that clears acetaldehyde. If that happens in people, it would let acetaldehyde build up faster than usual, which could explain why some people get a headache within an hour of just one or two glasses of red.

This is a hypothesis backed by lab work, not a proven cause, and the researchers have said human studies are needed. But it fits the pattern of red wine headaches better than sulfites do. Wine filters aren't marketed to remove quercetin, and there's no evidence they do.

### Tannins and other compounds

Tannins are the compounds that make red wine feel dry in your mouth. Some researchers have suggested they may trigger headaches in some people, possibly by affecting serotonin, but the evidence is limited. Red wine also contains other fermentation by-products, sometimes called congeners, that may make hangovers worse. Some filters may slightly change the wine's taste or texture, but they aren't designed to remove tannins.

### Migraine sensitivity

If you get migraines, red wine is one of the most commonly reported triggers. Migraine triggers are personal, and a filter is unlikely to change that. A doctor can help you work out whether wine is a real trigger for you and what to do about it.

### Drinking pattern

How fast you drink, whether you ate, and how much water you had all change how you feel later. These often matter more than anything in the wine itself. Our guide to [red wine headaches](/never-hungover/red-wine-headache) goes through each cause in more detail.

## PureWine vs Üllo vs Drops: Honest Pros and Cons

Here's a fair comparison based on what each product claims and how it works. We don't sell any of these, and we have no affiliate relationship with these brands.

| Product type | Removes sulfites | Removes histamine | Reusable | Main downsides |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| PureWine The Wand | Claimed | Claimed | No, one per glass | Ongoing cost; you have to wait a few minutes per glass |
| PureWine The Wave | Claimed | Claimed | No, one per bottle | Ongoing cost; single use creates waste |
| Üllo | Claimed (main focus) | Not its main claim | Yes, with replaceable filters | Higher upfront price; filters need replacing; slower pour |
| Hydrogen peroxide drops (e.g. SO2GO) | Yes, by chemical conversion | No | Bottle lasts many glasses | Sulfites only; you have to use the right amount |

### PureWine (Wand and Wave)

**Pros:**
- The only common option aimed at both sulfites and histamine, which is the better-supported of the two suspects.
- Easy to use at a restaurant or party, since the Wand fits in a pocket.
- The company says it doesn't change the taste, and many users say they can't tell the difference.

**Cons:**
- Single-use, so the cost per glass adds up if you drink wine often.
- Removal figures come from the company, not independent published studies.
- Does nothing about alcohol, quercetin, or how much you drink.

### Üllo

**Pros:**
- Reusable device, so the cost per glass can be lower over time if you drink a lot of wine.
- Aerates while it filters, which some people like for young red wines.
- Clear, focused claim: sulfite removal.

**Cons:**
- Mostly sulfite-focused, and sulfites are the weaker suspect for headaches.
- Higher upfront cost, plus replacement filters.
- Bulkier, so it's a home product more than a restaurant one.

### Wine drops

**Pros:**
- Usually the cheapest option per glass.
- The chemistry (hydrogen peroxide turning sulfite into sulfate) is simple and well understood.
- Small and easy to carry.

**Cons:**
- Only removes sulfites, not histamine.
- Some people notice a slight change in taste or aroma, especially if they add too much.
- Like the others, no published evidence that it reduces headaches.

### Which one, if any?

If you're curious and want to test the idea cheaply, drops are the lowest-cost experiment for sulfites. If you suspect histamine (you also react to aged cheese, cured meats, sauerkraut, or soy sauce), a product that targets histamine makes more sense to try. If wine gives you breathing trouble, skip the gadgets and see a doctor. If your headaches mostly show up after more than two or three glasses, no filter is likely to solve that.

## How to Test Whether a Wine Filter Works for You

Because there's no good evidence either way, your own careful test is the most useful thing you have. Here's a simple way to do it.

1. **Pick one wine that reliably gives you a headache.** Buy two bottles of the same wine, or use one bottle across two nights if you store it well.
2. **Keep everything else the same.** Same amount (measure it, for example two 5-ounce glasses), same time of night, eat a similar meal, and drink a similar amount of water.
3. **Do one night filtered and one night unfiltered.** Leave a few days between them.
4. **If you can, have someone else prepare the glass** so you don't know which night is filtered. This helps cut down on the placebo effect, which is strong with headaches.
5. **Write down what happens.** Note whether you got a headache, how soon, and how bad it was on a 1 to 10 scale.
6. **Repeat it once or twice.** One night proves very little. Two or three pairs give you a much clearer picture.

If the filtered nights are consistently better, the filter may be worth it for you. If there's no real difference, save your money and look at the other causes.

## Things That Help More Than Most Filters

These steps aren't as exciting as a gadget, but they address the causes that filters leave alone.

- **Pour smaller.** Measure a 5-ounce glass once so you know what it looks like. Many people are drinking 8 or 9 ounces and calling it one glass.
- **Choose lower-alcohol wines.** A 12% wine has noticeably less alcohol per glass than a 15% wine. Many European whites, some lighter reds like Gamay or Pinot Noir from cooler regions, and some sparkling wines sit on the lower end. Check the label.
- **Try a lighter or different red.** If the quercetin idea is right, wines from cooler, cloudier regions may contain less of it. That's a reasonable thing to experiment with, but there is no good evidence yet that it helps. Our guide to [wines that don't give you a headache](/never-hungover/wines-that-dont-give-you-a-headache) covers what to try.
- **Drink slowly and alternate with water.** A glass of water between glasses of wine slows you down and helps with hydration.
- **Eat with your wine.** Food slows how fast alcohol reaches your blood.
- **Notice your own pattern.** If one specific wine or style keeps giving you a headache and another doesn't, that's useful information, whatever the cause.

For a broader game plan, see our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover).

## Is Natural or Sulfite-Free Wine an Alternative to Filters?

Some people skip filters and buy wines labeled "no added sulfites" or "natural." That's a reasonable choice if you want fewer sulfites, but it has the same limit as a filter: it only helps if sulfites are your problem. Note that no wine is completely sulfite-free, because yeast naturally makes a small amount during fermentation. Natural wines can also contain more histamine and other fermentation by-products in some cases, so they aren't automatically gentler. And they still contain alcohol.

## When to See a Doctor

Most wine headaches in social drinkers come from the amount and type of wine, and they get better with water, food, and rest. But some reactions need a doctor, not a filter.

**See a doctor if:**

- Wine or other foods give you wheezing, chest tightness, hives, or flushing with a racing heart. That can be a sulfite or histamine reaction that needs proper testing.
- You get a headache from just a sip or a single small glass, every time.
- You have migraines and alcohol seems to set them off.
- Your headaches are getting more frequent or more severe.
- You get a strong facial flush, nausea, and a racing heart after small amounts of alcohol. This can be a sign of an inherited difference in how you break down alcohol.

**Call 911 or go to the emergency room if** you have trouble breathing, swelling of the lips, tongue, or throat, a sudden and severe headache that feels like the worst of your life, or a headache with confusion, weakness, a stiff neck, or trouble speaking.

## Where DHM Fits In

DHM (dihydromyricetin) is a plant compound that people often take for drinking nights. Unlike a filter, it isn't aimed at sulfites or histamine. Research on DHM has focused on how it may affect alcohol metabolism and the brain's response to alcohol, mostly in animal and lab studies, with limited human data. That's a different angle from filters, and it's promising but not proven. There's no good evidence that DHM prevents wine headaches, and it doesn't replace drinking less.

If you want to try it alongside the habits above, popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much to take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands.

## The Bottom Line

- Wine filters and drops mostly do remove sulfites, and some remove histamine too.
- There's no good evidence that they prevent wine headaches, and we couldn't find any independent clinical trial testing that.
- Sulfites are a weak suspect for most headaches. Histamine is a more plausible one for some people.
- Filters don't touch the likelier causes: the alcohol, quercetin in red grape skins, how much you drink, and migraine sensitivity.
- If you're curious, run a careful filtered-vs-unfiltered test at home. If wine gives you breathing trouble or hives, see a doctor instead.

If white wine is your trigger rather than red, our [white wine headache](/never-hungover/white-wine-headache) guide covers why it can still cause trouble even with fewer tannins and histamines.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Do wine filters really work?**

They mostly do what they claim chemically: they remove sulfites, and some also remove histamine. What hasn't been shown is that this prevents wine headaches. We couldn't find any independent clinical trial testing filters for headaches. Since sulfites aren't the main cause for most people, filters are likely to help only those who are actually sensitive to sulfites or histamine.

**Does PureWine actually work?**

PureWine's Wand and Wave are designed to remove both histamine and sulfites, and the company publishes its own test results showing large reductions. Independent evidence that this reduces headaches is lacking. PureWine makes the most sense to try if you suspect histamine sensitivity, for example if you also react to aged cheese or cured meats. It does not remove alcohol, so it won't help headaches caused by how much you drink.

**Is Üllo worth it?**

Üllo is a reusable pour-through device that mainly removes sulfites and also aerates the wine. It can be good value if you drink wine often and want to remove sulfites. But because sulfites are a weak suspect for most wine headaches, many people won't notice a difference. If you try it, compare filtered and unfiltered glasses of the same wine on separate nights.

**Do wine drops like SO2GO work?**

Most sulfite drops use a very dilute, food-grade hydrogen peroxide that converts sulfite into sulfate. That chemistry is real and well understood. Drops only target sulfites, not histamine, so they're only likely to help if sulfites are your trigger. They're the cheapest way to test whether removing sulfites makes any difference for you.

**Do wine filters remove alcohol?**

No. Wine filters and drops leave the alcohol in the wine. Since alcohol is the main driver of most wine headaches and hangovers, filtered wine can still give you a headache if you drink enough of it.

**Can a wine filter help with a sulfite allergy?**

Don't rely on one. Sulfite reactions can cause wheezing, chest tightness, and asthma attacks, and a filter may not remove every trace. If you've had a breathing reaction to wine, dried fruit, or other foods, see a doctor for proper advice, and follow their guidance on what to avoid and whether you need emergency medication.

**Do wine filters change the taste?**

Most companies say their products don't noticeably change the taste, and many users agree. Some people report a slight change in aroma or flavor, especially with drops if they add too much. Pour-through filters like Üllo also aerate the wine, which can soften young reds.

**What's the best way to avoid a wine headache?**

Drink less, pour smaller (about 5 ounces is a standard glass), pick lower-alcohol wines, eat with your wine, and have a glass of water between glasses. If red wine is the problem, try lighter reds or whites and note which ones bother you. A filter is fine to try as an experiment, but the habits above address the causes filters leave alone.
